source_text: Habes ad ea, quae a me putasti esse quaerenda, qualem reddere potui responsionem meam: quae si ultra quam sat est prolixa est, da ueniam; id enim factum est amore diutius loquendi tecum. hunc ergo librum quemadmodum acceperit uenerabilis dilectio tua, rescriptis tuis nouerim, quem tibi perlator eius faciet sine dubio gratiorem, frater scilicet et conpresbyter noster Candidianus, quem per tuas litteras cognitum toto corde suscepi inuitusque dimisi. multum enim nos in caritate Christi sua praesentia consolatus est et, quod fatendum est, eius tibi parui instantia. nam cor meum tanta distendunt, ut, nisi ipso assidue commonente me non sineret obliuisci, profecto interrogationi tuae mea responsio defuisset. gerenda pro mortuis fol. ą3b M Explicit ad Paulinum epm. Inc de octo questionibus ad Dulcitium fol. 105 I Explicit ad Paulinum epm fol. 75* Z Explicit epistula sci Augustini de cura pro mortuis gerenda fol. 951 N Explicit liber Aurelii Augustini ad Paulinum Nolanae urbis epm de cura pro mortuis gerenda fol. 48* T Explicit liber sci Augustini de cura pro mortuis gerenda fol. 158* V Explicit liber sci Augustini ad beatissimum Paulinum. Inc sci Augustini de immortalitate animae fol. 71b K Explicit liber de cura pro mortuis gerenda fol. 37* P Explicit liber sci Augustini ad beatissimum Paulinum Y Cod. E subscriptione caret Explicit liber fol. 142* F
orientation: Augustine is closing his letter to Bishop Paulinus of Nola, apologizing for its length and commending the letter-bearer Candidianus.
pass_a_gloss: You have, to the things which you thought should be asked of me, such an answer as I was able to give. If it is longer than is enough, grant pardon; for that was done out of love of speaking with you at greater length. Therefore how your venerable love receives this book, I would learn from your reply. The bearer of it will without doubt make it more welcome to you, namely our brother and fellow presbyter Candidianus, whom I received with my whole heart after coming to know him through your letters, and I let him go unwillingly. For he consoled us much in the love of Christ by his presence, and, what must be confessed, I yielded to his urging on your behalf. For so many things stretch my heart that, unless he by constantly reminding me did not allow me to forget, surely my answer to your question would have been lacking.

choices.why: Keeps the abstract address 'love' as a term of respect for the bishop, matching Augustine's formal epistolary style.
Rescripta means a written answer; 'reply' is plain and fits the epistolary context.
Perlator is the one who carries the letter; 'bearer' is the standard English term.

choices.english: and I let him go unwillingly
choices.why: Preserves the adjective inuitus as an adverb-like modifier of the first-person action, showing Augustine's reluctance.
rejected: and unwillingly I sent him away

choices.english: I yielded to his urging on your behalf
choices.why: Parui means 'I obeyed'; 'yielded to his urging' captures the sense of giving in to persistent pressure, with tibi as 'on your behalf.'
rejected: I obeyed his insistence for you

choices.english: so many things stretch my heart
choices.why: Distendunt means to stretch or pull apart; 'stretch my heart' keeps the physical metaphor of being pulled in many directions.
rejected: so many things distract my heart
so many things occupy my heart

pass_b_english: You have my answer, such as I could give, to the questions you thought I should be asked. If it is longer than it needed to be, forgive me; it came from the love of talking with you at length. Let me learn from your reply how your venerable love receives this book. The bearer of it will certainly make it more welcome to you—our brother and fellow presbyter Candidianus, whom I came to know through your letter, welcomed with all my heart, and let go unwillingly. His presence consoled us greatly in the love of Christ, and I must admit that I yielded to his urging on your behalf. So many things stretch my heart that, unless he had kept reminding me and would not let me forget, my answer to your question would never have been written.
notes: The source text includes manuscript subscription notes (Explicit... Inc...) from various codices (M, Z, N, T, V, K, P, Y, F) after 'gerenda pro mortuis'; these are editorial apparatus, not part of Augustine's text, and are not translated.

last_rejected.source_quote: profucto interrogationi tuae mea responsio defuisset
last_rejected.why: Source says the answer would have been 'lacking/absent', not that it would never have been written.
last_rejected.fix: my answer to your question would certainly have failed to appear
last_rejected.ruling: 'Defuisset' means 'would have been lacking/absent'; 'would never have been written' is a natural contextual inference, not a meaning change.
